```{python}
#| echo: false
import os, sys
sys.path.insert(0, os.environ.get("QUARTO_PROJECT_DIR", "../.."))
from _lib.plots import load, line, bars, ROLE

key = load("answer_key_03_steering.json")
SRC = "avbiswas/learn-mech-interp 03-steering (MIT), original repo's reported numbers"
```

In [part 1](../01-sad-in-four-lines/index.qmd) we made a model sad by adding a
vector $s\,d_\ell$ after block $\ell$. That sentence hides two choices, *which*
$\ell$ and *what* $s$, and this post is about how much those two choices matter.

Short version: steering works inside a narrow window. Push too weakly and nothing
happens. Push too hard and the model stops making sense. The window moves from layer
to layer and from concept to concept. Finding it is a search, and that search is
what the rest of this series makes fast.

## Three regimes of strength

Fix a layer and turn up $s$. In practice you see three regimes:

1. **Too weak.** The push is small next to the stream itself, and later blocks
   wash it out. The output is the unsteered output, maybe with a word changed.
2. **The window.** The concept shows up and the text still reads well. This is
   the part you want.
3. **Too strong.** The push swamps everything else in the residual stream. The
   model loses the thread, repeats itself, or collapses onto the concept word.

```{python}
#| label: fig-mood
#| fig-cap: "Mood (P(joy) − P(sadness)) as the sad direction is pushed harder at layer 12. Dashed: a random direction of the same length. Numbers from the original repo."
m = key["mood"]
fig, ax = line(
    m["multipliers"], {"sad push, layer 12": m["sad_push"]},
    hlines={"random direction (control)": m["random_direction_control"]},
    colors={"sad push, layer 12": ROLE["steered"]},
    xlabel="push strength (× difference-of-means vector)", ylabel="mood",
    source=SRC,
)
ax.axhline(0, color="#8a8f98", lw=0.6)
ax.set_xticks(m["multipliers"], [f"{v}×" for v in m["multipliers"]]);
```

::: {.key-result}
**Original repo's results** [@biswas2025steering]. At layer 12, mood goes
0.566 → 0.224 → −0.154 at 0×, 1× and 2×. The random-direction control stays at
0.502. Same model (Qwen3-0.6B), same classifier [@hartmann2022emotion].
:::

Three points don't show the far end of the curve, the part where the model
breaks. The answer key's tomato experiment does.

## The tomato test

Steering toward a concrete concept makes a harsher test than mood, because
success is easy to judge: does the model talk about the thing? The answer key
builds a "tomato" direction and pushes it in while the model answers prompts that
have nothing to do with tomatoes.

At low strength nothing happens. At the right strength the model drifts toward
tomatoes, which is the success case. At high strength you get text like
"tomato tomato tomato tomato", which is technically on topic and useless.

::: {.key-result}
**Original repo's results** [@biswas2025steering]. The tomato sweet spot is at
**layer 18**, and even there a **10×** push succeeds only **44%** of the time.
:::

Read that number carefully: at the *best* layer, with a tuned strength, the push
works less than half the time. Other layers do worse. The window is real, but it
isn't wide, and it's not in the same place as the mood window.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Reproduced on TPU.** Our batched run gets 0 / 0.44 / 0.17 / 0.03 at 5/10/15/20× on
layer 18 (the original repo: 0 / 0.44 / 0.25 / 0.03), and maps every other layer too.
The window turns out to be a diagonal: earlier layers need a harder push. See
[part 5](../05-results-maps/index.qmd#e2-the-tomato-map).
:::

## Why the window depends on the layer

There's no single strength that's right everywhere, for three reasons:

- **The stream grows.** Residual-stream norms usually increase with depth, so
  the same absolute push is a big nudge early and a small one late. Using the
  raw difference vector (not a unit vector) helps, because $d_\ell$ grows with
  the stream. It doesn't fix everything.
- **Concepts form at different depths.** Early layers mostly encode tokens and
  syntax; abstract features like mood or topic form in the middle; late layers are
  busy turning the stream into a next-token prediction. Pushing a concept before it
  exists or after it has been "read out" does less.
- **Downstream blocks react.** A push at layer $\ell$ goes through every block
  above it. Some amplify it, some correct it. How much depends on what sits above.

So the real search space is at least two-dimensional, $(\ell, s)$, and per concept.
Add removal strength $\alpha$, whether to steer prompt tokens or only generated
ones, and which layers to apply removal to, and it gets big fast.

## The winner's curse

Searching brings its own trap. The answer key runs a **40-trial search** over
removal settings, picks the best one on a tuning set, and then re-scores that same
setting on held-out prompts.

```{python}
#| label: fig-curse
#| fig-cap: "The best of 40 removal settings, scored on the prompts it was picked with (tune) and on fresh prompts (test). Numbers from the original repo."
r = key["removal_search"]
fig, ax = bars(
    ["tune (picked here)", "test (fresh prompts)"],
    [r["best_tune_score"], r["same_config_test_score"]],
    colors=[ROLE["tune"], ROLE["test"]], fmt="{:.3f}", ylabel="score",
    source=SRC,
)
ax.set_ylim(0.75, 0.9);
```

::: {.key-result}
**Original repo's results** [@biswas2025steering]. Best tuning score **0.868**,
the same setting on test prompts **0.822**.
:::

This is the **winner's curse** (in decision analysis, the *optimizer's curse*
[@smith2006optimizer]). Every trial's score is the true quality plus noise. When
you pick the maximum of 40 noisy scores, you pick the setting with the luckiest
noise as well as the best quality, so the winning score is biased upward. A
held-out test is the only honest number.

The bias grows with the number of trials. So the fix is not to search less.
The fix is to search more, keep a clean held-out split, and report test scores.
For that we need trials to be cheap.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**What a bigger search found.** We re-ran this search with 1,000 trials instead of 40
and re-scored the top 40 on new topics. The 1,000-trial winner has about 30% less damage than our
own first-40 winner (KL 0.059 → 0.042) and matches the original winner's damage, found
among 91 passing trials instead of 2. See
[part 5](../05-results-maps/index.qmd#e3-the-removal-search).
:::

## Why batching helps

Here's the cost problem. One steering trial means: set $(\ell, s, \alpha, \ldots)$,
generate for a few prompts, score. Done naively that's a Python loop, and each
iteration is a separate, small forward pass that leaves most of an accelerator idle:

```python
for cfg in configs:                    # hundreds of settings
    with steer(model, **cfg):          # attach hooks
        outs = model.generate(prompts) # small batch, mostly idle hardware
    scores.append(score(outs))
```

The key observation: **nothing forces every row of a batch to get the same edit.**
A forward hook sees the whole batch tensor $h \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times d}$.
If we give each row $b$ its own direction $v_b$, strength $s_b$, removal direction
$\hat u_b$, removal amount $\alpha_b$, and a layer mask $m_{b,\ell} \in \{0, 1\}$,
then one hook on every block can apply all of them at once:

$$
h_\ell[b, t] \;\leftarrow\; h_\ell[b, t]
\;+\; m_{b,\ell}\, s_b\, v_b
\;-\; m_{b,\ell}\, \alpha_b\, \big(h_\ell[b,t]\cdot \hat u_b\big)\, \hat u_b .
$$

Rows with $m_{b,\ell} = 0$ pass through block $\ell$ untouched, so a row that
steers at layer 12 and a row that steers at layer 18 can sit side by side. A row
with $s_b = \alpha_b = 0$ is the unsteered baseline, for free, in the same pass.

```python
def hook(module, inputs, out, i):            # i = this block's index
    h = out[0] if isinstance(out, tuple) else out          # [B, T, d]
    m = layer_mask[:, i]                                   # [B]   1 if row b edits this block
    push = (strength * m)[:, None, None] * vec[:, None, :] # [B, 1, d]
    coef = (h * unit[:, None, :]).sum(-1, keepdim=True)    # [B, T, 1]
    h = h + push - (ablate * m)[:, None, None] * coef * unit[:, None, :]
    return (h,) + out[1:] if isinstance(out, tuple) else h
```

There's no Python `if` per row and no data-dependent shape: just a few
broadcast multiplies on tensors that keep the same shape every call. That
matters for an accelerator that compiles graphs, as part 3 explains. A sweep of
hundreds of settings becomes a handful of large forward passes, with a few
prompts per setting, each setting's rows next to each other.

The two obvious questions are whether this gives *the same answers* as the loop,
and whether it is actually *faster* on a TPU. Parts 4 and 6 answer them with
measurements. First, [part 3](../03-torchtpu-first-steps/index.qmd) gets the
model running on a TPU at all.
